title: Inference & Regression
description: Confidence intervals and sample size; hypothesis tests, p-values, Type I/II errors and power; z, t and paired procedures; two-sample comparisons, ANOVA and chi-square tests; correlation, least-squares regression and inference for the slope.

cards.title: What do $H_0$ and $H_a$ represent, and which one contains the equals sign?
cards.body:
$H_0$ is the null (it holds the equality); $H_a$ is the alternative.

The **null hypothesis** is the skeptical "no effect, no difference" claim, e.g. $H_0: \mu = 50$. The **alternative hypothesis** is what the study seeks evidence for: $\mu \ne 50$, $\mu < 50$ or $\mu > 50$.

Watch out: both are statements about parameters ($\mu$, $p$), never sample statistics ($\bar{x}$, $\hat{p}$).
Tip: write $H_0$ and $H_a$ before looking at the data.
cards.searchQuery: null hypothesis alternative hypothesis equals sign

cards.title: What exactly is a p-value?
cards.body:
The probability, assuming $H_0$ is true, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed.

"Extreme" means in the direction of $H_a$: one tail for a one-sided test, both tails for a two-sided test. A small **p-value** means the data would be surprising if $H_0$ were true.

Watch out: it is not the probability that $H_0$ is true, and not the probability that the result is due to chance alone.
Key idea: the p-value measures how well the data fit $H_0$, not how likely $H_0$ is.
cards.searchQuery: p-value definition probability assuming null true

cards.title: A test at $\alpha = 0.05$ gives $p = 0.08$. What is the correct conclusion?
cards.body:
Fail to reject $H_0$: the data do not provide convincing evidence for $H_a$.

Since $p = 0.08 > \alpha = 0.05$, the result is not statistically significant at the $5\%$ level, so we **fail to reject** $H_0$.

Watch out: never write "accept $H_0$" or "$H_0$ is true". A large p-value means insufficient evidence against $H_0$, not proof of it.
cards.searchQuery: fail to reject null hypothesis p value greater than alpha

cards.title: Rejecting $H_0$ when $H_0$ is actually true is which type of error?
cards.body:
Type I error, a false positive.

Its probability is $\alpha$: at $\alpha = 0.05$, a true $H_0$ is wrongly rejected $5\%$ of the time. A **Type II error** is failing to reject a false $H_0$; its probability is $\beta$.

Mnemonic: Type I is the false alarm, like convicting an innocent defendant.
cards.searchQuery: Type I error false positive reject true null

cards.title: A test has $P(\text{Type II error}) = \beta = 0.2$. What is its power?
cards.body:
$0.8$.

**Power** $= 1 - \beta = P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ false})$: the chance of detecting a real effect.

Tip: power rises with a larger $n$, a larger true effect, a larger $\alpha$ or less variability. Increasing $n$ is usually the practical lever.
cards.searchQuery: statistical power 1 minus beta Type II error

cards.title: With known $\sigma = 12$ and $n = 36$, what is the margin of error of a $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$?
cards.body:
$3.92$.

$\mathrm{ME} = z^*\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = 1.96 \times \dfrac{12}{\sqrt{36}} = 1.96 \times 2 = 3.92$, so the **confidence interval** is $\bar{x} \pm 3.92$.

Tip: other levels use $z^* = 1.645$ for $90\%$ and $z^* = 2.576$ for $99\%$.
cards.searchQuery: margin of error 95% confidence interval known sigma

cards.title: What does the '$95\%$' in a $95\%$ confidence interval actually mean?
cards.body:
The method's long-run **success rate**.

If we took many random samples and built a $95\%$ CI from each, about $95\%$ of those intervals would contain the true parameter.

Watch out: it does not mean "a $95\%$ chance $\mu$ is in this interval" ($\mu$ is fixed; this interval either contains it or not), nor that $95\%$ of the data fall in it.
cards.searchQuery: interpret 95% confidence interval meaning

cards.title: To cut a confidence interval's margin of error in half (same confidence level), multiply the sample size by what?
cards.body:
$4$.

$\mathrm{ME} = z^*\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is proportional to $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$, so halving it means doubling $\sqrt{n}$, which takes **four times** as many observations.

Example: going from $n = 100$ to $n = 400$ cuts the margin of error in half.
Watch out: merely doubling $n$ shrinks the margin of error by a factor of only $\sqrt{2}$.
cards.searchQuery: halve margin of error sample size four times

cards.title: Blood pressure is measured on the same $20$ patients before and after a drug. Which $t$-test fits: paired or two-sample?
cards.body:
Paired.

Each patient gives two linked measurements, so take the **differences** (after minus before) and run a one-sample $t$-test on their mean, with $\mathrm{df} = 20 - 1 = 19$.

Watch out: a two-sample $t$-test is for two independent groups. Using it on paired data ignores the pairing and throws away power.
cards.searchQuery: paired t-test versus two-sample t-test before after

cards.title: A chi-square test of independence uses a table with $3$ rows and $4$ columns. How many degrees of freedom?
cards.body:
$6$.

$\mathrm{df} = (r-1)(c-1) = (3-1)(4-1) = 6$.

Watch out: do not count the totals row or column.
Tip: each expected count is $\dfrac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{\text{table total}}$, and every expected count should be at least $5$.
cards.searchQuery: chi-square test of independence degrees of freedom

cards.title: What values can the correlation coefficient $r$ take, and what does $r = -0.9$ indicate?
cards.body:
Any value from $-1$ to $1$; $r = -0.9$ is a strong negative linear association.

The sign gives the direction and the size gives the strength of the **linear** association. $r$ has no units and does not change if you swap $x$ and $y$ or change units.

Watch out: $r \approx 0$ can hide a strong curved pattern, because $r$ measures only linear association.
cards.searchQuery: correlation coefficient r range strength direction

cards.title: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths are strongly correlated. Why can't we conclude ice cream causes drowning?
cards.body:
Correlation does not imply causation.

A **lurking (confounding) variable**, hot weather, drives both ice cream sales and swimming, and so drowning risk.

Key idea: only a randomized experiment can establish cause and effect; observational data like these show association only.
cards.searchQuery: correlation does not imply causation confounding variable

cards.title: $r = 0.8$, $s_x = 5$, and $s_y = 10$. What is the least-squares slope $b_1$ for predicting $y$ from $x$?
cards.body:
$1.6$.

$b_1 = r\dfrac{s_y}{s_x} = 0.8 \times \dfrac{10}{5} = 1.6$. Each $1$-unit increase in $x$ predicts a $1.6$-unit increase in $y$, on average.

Tip: the **slope** always has the same sign as $r$.
cards.searchQuery: least squares slope r times sy over sx

cards.title: A least-squares line has slope $b_1 = 3$, and the data have $\bar{x} = 10$ and $\bar{y} = 50$. What is the intercept $b_0$?
cards.body:
$20$.

The least-squares line always passes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$, so $b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1\bar{x} = 50 - 3(10) = 20$, giving $\hat{y} = 20 + 3x$.

Tip: if you know $b_1$, $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$, the **intercept** takes one line of arithmetic.
cards.searchQuery: least squares intercept y bar minus slope x bar

cards.title: Using $\hat{y} = 20 + 3x$, a data point has $x = 10$ and observed $y = 47$. What is its residual?
cards.body:
$-3$.

**Residual** $=$ observed $-$ predicted: $e = y - \hat{y} = 47 - (20 + 30) = -3$.

Watch out: a negative residual means the point lies below the line (the model overestimated it).
Key idea: least squares minimizes the sum of the squared residuals.
cards.searchQuery: residual observed minus predicted regression

cards.title: A linear regression has $r = 0.6$. What fraction of the variation in $y$ is explained by the model?
cards.body:
$0.36$, i.e. $36\%$.

$R^2 = r^2 = 0.6^2 = 0.36$: $36\%$ of the variability in $y$ is accounted for by the linear relationship with $x$.

Watch out: it does not mean that $36\%$ of the points fall on the line.
cards.searchQuery: r squared coefficient of determination explained variation

cards.title: What is a point estimate, and how does it differ from an interval estimate?
cards.body:
A point estimate is a single number computed from the sample (such as $\bar{x}$ or $\hat{p}$) that estimates a parameter.

An **interval estimate** adds a margin of error to say how precise that single number is: $\text{estimate} \pm \text{margin of error}$.

Key idea: a point estimate almost never equals the parameter exactly, which is why we report a confidence interval alongside it.
cards.searchQuery: point estimate versus interval estimate confidence interval

cards.title: What is the formula for a confidence interval for $\mu$ when $\sigma$ is known?
cards.body:
$\bar{x} \pm z^*\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$

The **critical value** $z^*$ sets the confidence level, and $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is the standard error of $\bar{x}$.

Tip: in practice $\sigma$ is rarely known, so the $t$ interval $\bar{x} \pm t^*\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ is used far more often.
cards.searchQuery: confidence interval mean known sigma formula z critical value

cards.title: What three things determine the margin of error of a confidence interval for a mean, and in which direction does each push it?
cards.body:
A higher confidence level and a larger $\sigma$ widen it; a larger $n$ narrows it.

In $\mathrm{ME} = z^*\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$, a higher confidence level means a larger $z^*$, more variability means a larger $\sigma$, and a larger sample size shrinks the **standard error**.

Watch out: the margin of error accounts only for sampling variability, not for bias from a poorly designed sample.
cards.searchQuery: margin of error factors confidence level variability sample size

cards.title: What is the standard deviation of $\hat{p}$ when $p = 0.5$ and $n = 100$?
cards.body:
$0.05$.

$\sqrt{\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.5 \times 0.5}{100}} = \sqrt{0.0025} = 0.05$.

Tip: for a confidence interval, use $\hat{p}$ in place of $p$ to get the **standard error**; for a test of $H_0: p = p_0$, use $p_0$.
cards.searchQuery: standard deviation of sample proportion p hat formula

cards.title: What is the critical value $z^*$ for a $90\%$ confidence interval? Use the standard table value.
cards.body:
$1.645$.

The middle $90\%$ of a standard normal lies between $-1.645$ and $1.645$, leaving $5\%$ in each tail.

Tip: memorize $1.645$, $1.96$ and $2.576$ for $90\%$, $95\%$ and $99\%$ confidence.
cards.searchQuery: z critical value 90 percent confidence interval 1.645

cards.title: What critical value $z^*$ gives a $95\%$ confidence interval for a mean when $\sigma$ is known?
cards.body:
$1.96$.

The middle $95\%$ of a standard normal lies between $-1.96$ and $1.96$, leaving $2.5\%$ in each tail.

Tip: back-of-envelope intervals round $z^*$ to $2$, which is why "estimate $\pm$ two standard errors" is a popular rule of thumb.
cards.searchQuery: z critical value 95 percent confidence interval 1.96

cards.title: What is the critical value $z^*$ for a $99\%$ confidence interval? Use the standard table value.
cards.body:
$2.576$.

The middle $99\%$ of a standard normal lies between $-2.576$ and $2.576$, leaving $0.5\%$ in each tail.

Watch out: a higher confidence level means a larger $z^*$ and a wider interval.
cards.searchQuery: z critical value 99 percent confidence interval 2.576

cards.title: A sample of $n = 25$ has $\bar{x} = 50$ and known $\sigma = 10$. What is the lower endpoint of the $95\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$? Use $z^* = 1.96$.
cards.body:
$46.08$.

$\mathrm{SE} = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{25}} = 2$, so $\mathrm{ME} = 1.96 \times 2 = 3.92$ and the interval is $50 \pm 3.92 = (46.08,\ 53.92)$.

Tip: compute the **standard error** first, then multiply by $z^*$, then add and subtract.
cards.searchQuery: confidence interval lower endpoint z interval worked example

cards.title: With the sample size fixed, what happens to the width of a confidence interval when you raise the confidence level from $95\%$ to $99\%$?
cards.body:
It gets wider.

A larger critical value ($2.576$ instead of $1.96$) multiplies the same standard error. You buy more confidence by giving up **precision**.

Tip: to gain both confidence and precision, you need a larger sample.
cards.searchQuery: confidence level width wider interval trade off precision

cards.title: How large a sample is needed to estimate $\mu$ within $\pm 3$ at $95\%$ confidence if $\sigma = 15$? Round up to a whole number.
cards.body:
$97$.

$n = \left(\dfrac{z^*\sigma}{E}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{1.96 \times 15}{3}\right)^2 = 9.8^2 = 96.04$.

Watch out: always round **up**. Rounding $96.04$ down to $96$ would miss the target margin of error.
cards.searchQuery: sample size for estimating mean margin of error formula

cards.title: Using the conservative value $\hat{p} = 0.5$, how large must $n$ be for a $95\%$ confidence interval for a proportion with a margin of error of $0.03$? Round up.
cards.body:
$1068$.

$n = \left(\dfrac{z^*}{E}\right)^2 \hat{p}(1-\hat{p}) = \left(\dfrac{1.96}{0.03}\right)^2 (0.25) \approx 1067.1$.

Why: $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$ is largest at $\hat{p} = 0.5$, so this choice guarantees the target margin of error whatever the true $p$ is.
Watch out: round **up** to $1068$.
cards.searchQuery: sample size proportion conservative p 0.5 margin of error

cards.title: What is the formula for a $t$ confidence interval for a mean, and how many degrees of freedom does it use?
cards.body:
$\bar{x} \pm t^*\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$, with $\mathrm{df} = n - 1$.

Use the sample standard deviation $s$ in the **standard error** $\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ and find $t^*$ for the confidence level and $\mathrm{df}$.

Tip: for the same confidence level, $t^*$ is larger than $z^*$, so a $t$ interval is slightly wider.
cards.searchQuery: t confidence interval mean formula degrees of freedom

cards.title: $\bar{x} = 20$, $s = 5$, $n = 16$. What is the margin of error of a $95\%$ $t$ interval? Use $t^* = 2.131$ and round to 2 decimals.
cards.body:
$2.66$.

$\mathrm{ME} = t^*\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = 2.131 \times \dfrac{5}{4} = 2.664$, so the CI is $20 \pm 2.66 = (17.34,\ 22.66)$.

Watch out: $t^* = 2.131$ comes from $\mathrm{df} = 16 - 1 = 15$, not from $n$.
cards.searchQuery: t interval margin of error worked example sample standard deviation

cards.title: What conditions should hold before you use a $t$ interval for a mean?
cards.body:
The sample is random, the observations are independent, and the data are approximately normal (or $n$ is large).

- **Random**: a random sample or randomized experiment.
- **Independent**: when sampling without replacement, the sample is under $10\%$ of the population.
- **Normal**: the population is roughly normal, or $n \ge 30$. For a small sample, check a plot for strong skew and outliers.

Watch out: a large sample does not repair a biased sampling method.
cards.searchQuery: conditions for t interval random independent normal 10 percent

cards.title: $\hat{p} = 0.4$ from a sample of $n = 100$. What is the margin of error of a $95\%$ confidence interval for $p$? Round to 3 decimals.
cards.body:
$0.096$.

$\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.4 \times 0.6}{100}} \approx 0.049$, so $\mathrm{ME} = 1.96 \times 0.049 \approx 0.096$.

Tip: the interval is $0.4 \pm 0.096 = (0.304,\ 0.496)$.
cards.searchQuery: proportion confidence interval margin of error worked example

cards.title: What is the success-failure condition for a confidence interval for a proportion?
cards.body:
$n\hat{p} \ge 10$ and $n(1-\hat{p}) \ge 10$.

It guarantees that the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ is close enough to **normal** for $z$ methods to work. The sample must also be random, with the observations independent.

Watch out: for a test of $H_0: p = p_0$, check $np_0 \ge 10$ and $n(1-p_0) \ge 10$ instead.
cards.searchQuery: success failure condition proportion confidence interval np at least 10

cards.title: A $95\%$ CI for $\mu$ is $(12, 18)$. Would a two-sided test of $H_0: \mu = 20$ at $\alpha = 0.05$ reject $H_0$? Answer yes or no.
cards.body:
Yes.

The value $20$ lies outside the interval, so it is not a plausible value for $\mu$ at the $95\%$ level, and the two-sided test at $\alpha = 0.05$ **rejects** $H_0$.

Key idea: a $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval and a two-sided test at level $\alpha$ agree: reject exactly when the null value falls outside the interval.
cards.searchQuery: confidence interval two-sided hypothesis test equivalence reject null value

cards.title: What is the test statistic for a one-sample $z$ test of $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$ when $\sigma$ is known?
cards.body:
$z = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$

It counts how many **standard errors** the sample mean lies from the hypothesized mean. Large $|z|$ means the data are far from what $H_0$ predicts.

Tip: every test statistic has the form $\dfrac{\text{estimate} - \text{null value}}{\text{standard error}}$.
cards.searchQuery: one-sample z test statistic formula known sigma

cards.title: $\bar{x} = 52$, $\mu_0 = 50$, $\sigma = 10$, $n = 25$. What is the $z$ statistic?
cards.body:
$1$.

$\mathrm{SE} = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{25}} = 2$, so $z = \dfrac{52 - 50}{2} = 1$.

Watch out: divide by the standard error $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$, not by $\sigma$.
cards.searchQuery: z statistic worked example sample mean hypothesized mean

cards.title: What is the test statistic for a one-sample $t$ test of $H_0: \mu = \mu_0$, and how many degrees of freedom does it have?
cards.body:
$t = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}$, with $\mathrm{df} = n - 1$.

It has the same form as $z$, but uses the sample standard deviation $s$, which adds uncertainty and gives the **$t$ distribution** heavier tails.

Tip: for large $n$ the $t$ and $z$ results are nearly identical.
cards.searchQuery: one-sample t test statistic formula degrees of freedom

cards.title: $\bar{x} = 105$, $\mu_0 = 100$, $s = 15$, $n = 36$. What is the $t$ statistic?
cards.body:
$2$.

$\mathrm{SE} = \dfrac{15}{\sqrt{36}} = 2.5$, so $t = \dfrac{105 - 100}{2.5} = 2$, with $\mathrm{df} = 35$.

Watch out: $\sqrt{36} = 6$; forgetting the square root of $n$ is a classic slip.
cards.searchQuery: t statistic worked example one-sample sample standard deviation

cards.title: In a two-sided $z$ test, $z = 1.96$. What is the p-value? Round to 2 decimals.
cards.body:
$0.05$.

The upper tail beyond $1.96$ has area $0.025$; a two-sided test counts both tails, so $p = 2(0.025) = 0.05$.

Watch out: forgetting to double the tail area is the most common two-sided error.
cards.searchQuery: two-sided z test p-value 1.96 both tails

cards.title: For $H_a: \mu > \mu_0$ the $z$ statistic is $1.645$. What is the p-value? Round to 2 decimals.
cards.body:
$0.05$.

For a right-tailed test the p-value is just the upper-tail area beyond the statistic: $P(Z > 1.645) = 0.05$.

Key idea: one-sided tests use one tail; two-sided tests double it.
cards.searchQuery: right-tailed z test p-value 1.645 upper tail

cards.title: To reject $H_0$ in a right-tailed $z$ test at $\alpha = 0.05$, the statistic must exceed what critical value?
cards.body:
$1.645$.

All $5\%$ of the rejection region sits in the upper tail, so the cutoff is the $95$th percentile of the standard normal.

Tip: the **rejection region** approach and the p-value approach always give the same decision.
cards.searchQuery: critical value right-tailed z test alpha 0.05 rejection region

cards.title: To reject $H_0$ in a two-sided $z$ test at $\alpha = 0.01$, $|z|$ must exceed what critical value?
cards.body:
$2.576$.

Split $\alpha$ between the tails: $0.005$ in each, so the cutoffs are $\pm 2.576$.

Tip: the same value appears in a $99\%$ confidence interval, because a $99\%$ interval corresponds to a two-sided test at $\alpha = 0.01$.
cards.searchQuery: two-sided z test critical value alpha 0.01 2.576

cards.title: How do you decide whether to reject $H_0$ using the p-value and the significance level $\alpha$?
cards.body:
Reject $H_0$ when $p \le \alpha$; otherwise fail to reject.

If $p \le \alpha$ the result is **statistically significant**: data this extreme would be rare if $H_0$ were true.

Watch out: choose $\alpha$ before collecting data, not after seeing the p-value.
cards.searchQuery: hypothesis test decision rule p-value less than alpha reject

cards.title: When should you use a one-sided alternative instead of a two-sided one?
cards.body:
Only when the research question, stated before seeing the data, cares about a difference in one direction alone.

The default is **two-sided**: $H_a: \mu \ne \mu_0$. A one-sided test puts all of $\alpha$ in one tail, so it is easier to reject in that direction but blind to the other.

Watch out: switching to a one-sided test after seeing which way the data point is cheating.
cards.searchQuery: one-sided versus two-sided alternative hypothesis when to use

cards.title: A huge study finds a statistically significant difference that is tiny in size. What does this illustrate?
cards.body:
Statistical significance is not the same as **practical significance**.

With a very large $n$ the standard error is tiny, so even a trivial difference gives a small p-value.

Tip: always report the size of the effect, for instance with a confidence interval, not just the p-value.
cards.searchQuery: statistical significance versus practical significance large sample

cards.title: Failing to reject a false $H_0$ is which type of error?
cards.body:
Type II error, a false negative.

Its probability is $\beta$, and power is $1 - \beta$. A **Type I error** is rejecting a true $H_0$.

Mnemonic: Type II is a miss: the effect was real, but the test missed it.
cards.searchQuery: Type II error false negative fail to reject false null

cards.title: With $n$ fixed, you lower $\alpha$ from $0.05$ to $0.01$. Does $\beta$ increase or decrease?
cards.body:
It increases, so power falls.

A smaller $\alpha$ makes the rejection region smaller, which makes it harder to reject, even when $H_0$ is false.

Tip: the only way to reduce both error rates at once is to increase $n$.
cards.searchQuery: alpha beta tradeoff lower significance level type II error increases

cards.title: Which one of these lowers the power of a test: a larger $n$, a larger true effect, or a smaller $\alpha$?
cards.body:
A smaller $\alpha$.

A larger $n$ shrinks the standard error and a larger true effect moves the statistic further from $H_0$; both **raise** power. A smaller $\alpha$ makes rejection harder.

Tip: less variability in the data also raises power.
cards.searchQuery: factors affecting power hypothesis test sample size alpha

cards.title: You run $20$ independent tests, each at $\alpha = 0.05$, and every null hypothesis is true. About how many false positives do you expect?
cards.body:
$1$.

The expected count is $20 \times 0.05 = 1$, and the chance of at least one false positive is $1 - 0.95^{20} \approx 0.64$.

Watch out: running many tests and reporting only the significant ones inflates the **Type I error** rate. Adjust, for example with a Bonferroni correction ($\alpha/20$).
cards.searchQuery: multiple comparisons false positives 20 tests alpha 0.05

cards.title: What is the test statistic for a one-proportion $z$ test of $H_0: p = p_0$?
cards.body:
$z = \dfrac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}$

The **standard error** uses the null value $p_0$, because the test assumes $H_0$ is true.

Watch out: a confidence interval for $p$ uses $\hat{p}$ in its standard error; the test uses $p_0$.
cards.searchQuery: one-proportion z test statistic formula p0

cards.title: $H_0: p = 0.5$ with $\hat{p} = 0.56$ and $n = 100$. What is the $z$ statistic?
cards.body:
$1.2$.

$\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.5 \times 0.5}{100}} = 0.05$, so $z = \dfrac{0.56 - 0.5}{0.05} = 1.2$.

Tip: with $z = 1.2$ the two-sided p-value is about $0.23$, so there is no convincing evidence against $H_0$.
cards.searchQuery: one-proportion z test worked example p hat p0

cards.title: A test of $H_0: p = 0.5$ gives a p-value of $0.03$ at $\alpha = 0.05$. How should you state the conclusion?
cards.body:
Reject $H_0$: there is convincing evidence that the true proportion differs from $0.5$.

A good conclusion has three parts: the **decision** (reject or fail to reject), a link to the p-value and $\alpha$, and a statement about the claim in context.

Watch out: do not write that "$H_a$ is proven" or that there is a $3\%$ chance $H_0$ is true.
cards.searchQuery: hypothesis test conclusion in context reject null p-value 0.03

cards.title: Paired differences have $\bar{d} = 2.5$, $s_d = 5$ and $n = 25$. What is $t$ for $H_0: \mu_d = 0$?
cards.body:
$2.5$.

$\mathrm{SE} = \dfrac{5}{\sqrt{25}} = 1$, so $t = \dfrac{2.5 - 0}{1} = 2.5$, with $\mathrm{df} = 24$.

Tip: a paired test is just a one-sample $t$ test on the **differences**.
cards.searchQuery: paired t test statistic worked example mean difference

cards.title: Why can a paired design be more powerful than two independent samples?
cards.body:
Differences within each pair cancel out person-to-person variability.

Subjects (or twins, or before-and-after measurements) serve as their own **controls**, so the standard error of the mean difference is smaller and real effects are easier to detect.

Watch out: pairing only helps when the paired measurements are positively correlated.
cards.searchQuery: paired design advantage matched pairs reduces variability

cards.title: What is the bootstrap, and what does it approximate?
cards.body:
Resampling with replacement from the observed sample, many times, to approximate the sampling distribution of a statistic.

Each **resample** has the same size as the original sample; computing the statistic for each gives an estimate of its standard error or a confidence interval.

Tip: it needs no normality assumption, which makes it useful for statistics like the median.
cards.searchQuery: bootstrap resampling with replacement sampling distribution

cards.title: How does a permutation test judge whether two groups differ?
cards.body:
Shuffle the group labels many times and see how often the shuffled difference is as large as the observed one.

If $H_0$ (the labels do not matter) were true, any shuffle is equally likely. The fraction of shuffles at least as extreme as the observed result is the **p-value**.

Tip: like the bootstrap, it needs no normality assumption.
cards.searchQuery: permutation test shuffle group labels p-value

cards.title: What does random assignment of subjects to treatments allow that random sampling alone does not?
cards.body:
Conclusions about **cause and effect**.

Random assignment balances lurking variables across groups on average, so a difference in outcomes can be attributed to the treatment. Random sampling, by contrast, lets you generalize to the population.

Key idea: random sampling supports generalization; random assignment supports causation.
cards.searchQuery: random assignment versus random sampling cause and effect experiment

cards.title: Two groups means differ by $5$ and the pooled standard deviation is $10$. What is Cohen's $d$?
cards.body:
$0.5$.

$d = \dfrac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p} = \dfrac{5}{10} = 0.5$: the difference measured in standard deviations.

Tip: rough benchmarks are $0.2$ small, $0.5$ medium and $0.8$ large. Unlike a p-value, an **effect size** does not shrink or grow with $n$.
cards.searchQuery: Cohen's d effect size difference in means pooled standard deviation

cards.title: Two independent samples have $s_1 = 12$, $n_1 = 16$, $s_2 = 16$ and $n_2 = 16$. What is the standard error $\sqrt{\dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{n_2}}$ of $\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2$?
cards.body:
$5$.

$\dfrac{12^2}{16} = 9$ and $\dfrac{16^2}{16} = 16$, so $\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5$.

Key idea: the **variances** of independent estimates add, so add the squared standard errors and then take the square root.
cards.searchQuery: two-sample t standard error difference of means formula

cards.title: Two independent groups give $\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 = 10$ with standard error $5$. What is the two-sample $t$ statistic for $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$?
cards.body:
$2$.

$t = \dfrac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) - 0}{\mathrm{SE}} = \dfrac{10}{5} = 2$.

Tip: the null value for the difference is $0$, so it drops out of the numerator.
cards.searchQuery: two-sample t statistic worked example difference in means

cards.title: For a two-sample $t$ procedure with $n_1 = 12$ and $n_2 = 20$, what is the conservative degrees of freedom, $\min(n_1 - 1,\ n_2 - 1)$?
cards.body:
$11$.

$\min(12 - 1,\ 20 - 1) = \min(11, 19) = 11$.

Watch out: software uses the more precise **Welch** formula, which gives a non-integer between $11$ and $30$; the minimum is the safe by-hand choice.
cards.searchQuery: two-sample t degrees of freedom conservative minimum n minus 1

cards.title: What conditions should hold for a two-sample $t$ procedure comparing two means?
cards.body:
Two independent random samples (or two randomly assigned groups), each approximately normal or large.

- **Random**: each sample is random, or subjects are randomly assigned.
- **Independent**: the two groups are independent of each other and each is under $10\%$ of its population.
- **Normal**: each population is roughly normal, or each $n \ge 30$.

Watch out: if the measurements are naturally linked in pairs, use a paired test instead.
cards.searchQuery: two-sample t test conditions independent groups normal

cards.title: A $95\%$ CI for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ is $(-1.2,\ 4.6)$. Does a two-sided test of $H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2$ at $\alpha = 0.05$ reject $H_0$? Answer yes or no.
cards.body:
No.

The interval contains $0$, so "no difference" is a plausible value, and the test **fails to reject** $H_0$.

Tip: the interval also shows the plausible size and direction of the difference, which a p-value cannot.
cards.searchQuery: confidence interval difference of means contains zero no significant difference

cards.title: Group 1 has $30$ successes in $n_1 = 100$ and group 2 has $50$ in $n_2 = 150$. What is the pooled proportion $\hat{p}$ for a two-proportion $z$ test?
cards.body:
$0.32$.

$\hat{p} = \dfrac{30 + 50}{100 + 150} = \dfrac{80}{250} = 0.32$.

Key idea: under $H_0: p_1 = p_2$ there is one common proportion, and the **pooled** estimate uses all of the data.
cards.searchQuery: pooled proportion two-proportion z test formula

cards.title: Why does a two-proportion $z$ test pool the samples, while a confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$ does not?
cards.body:
The test assumes $H_0: p_1 = p_2$, so one **common** proportion best describes both groups; the interval makes no such assumption.

A confidence interval estimates the actual difference, so each group keeps its own $\hat{p}_i$ in the standard error.

Tip: the same logic explains why a one-proportion test uses $p_0$ in its standard error while the interval uses $\hat{p}$.
cards.searchQuery: two proportion test pooled versus confidence interval unpooled standard error

cards.title: $25$ pairs of twins are studied; within each pair, one twin is randomly assigned a new treatment and the other a placebo. Which procedure compares the treatments: paired or two-sample?
cards.body:
Paired.

The twins in each pair are linked, so analyze the $25$ **differences** with a one-sample $t$ procedure ($\mathrm{df} = 24$).

Watch out: random assignment within each pair is still a paired design; what matters is that the observations are matched.
cards.searchQuery: paired design matched pairs twins t test

cards.title: $\hat{p}_1 = 0.5$ with $n_1 = 100$, and $\hat{p}_2 = 0.4$ with $n_2 = 100$. What is the unpooled standard error of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$?
cards.body:
$0.07$.

$\mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.5 \times 0.5}{100} + \dfrac{0.4 \times 0.6}{100}} = \sqrt{0.0025 + 0.0024} = \sqrt{0.0049} = 0.07$.

Tip: this is the **standard error** used for a confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$.
cards.searchQuery: standard error difference of two proportions confidence interval

cards.title: A $95\%$ CI for $p_1 - p_2$ is $0.10 \pm 1.96(0.07) = (-0.037,\ 0.237)$. Does it give convincing evidence that the proportions differ? Answer yes or no.
cards.body:
No.

The interval includes $0$, so $p_1 = p_2$ is plausible at the $95\%$ level, even though $\hat{p}_1 > \hat{p}_2$ in the sample.

Watch out: a sample difference of $0.10$ is not evidence of a population difference when the interval is that wide.
cards.searchQuery: two proportion confidence interval includes zero evidence of difference

cards.title: What are the hypotheses of a one-way ANOVA comparing $k$ group means?
cards.body:
$H_0$: all $k$ population means are equal. $H_a$: at least one mean differs.

ANOVA tests the **null hypothesis** $\mu_1 = \mu_2 = \cdots = \mu_k$ with a single $F$ test.

Watch out: $H_a$ does not say that all means differ, only that they are not all equal.
cards.searchQuery: one-way ANOVA null alternative hypotheses all means equal

cards.title: Why run one ANOVA instead of many two-sample $t$ tests when comparing several means?
cards.body:
Many separate tests inflate the overall Type I error rate.

With $k = 4$ groups there are $6$ pairs; at $\alpha = 0.05$ each, the chance of at least one false positive is far above $5\%$. One **$F$ test** keeps the overall error rate at $\alpha$.

Tip: if the $F$ test is significant, follow up with a post hoc procedure to see which means differ.
cards.searchQuery: ANOVA versus multiple t tests type I error inflation

cards.title: What ratio defines the $F$ statistic in a one-way ANOVA?
cards.body:
$F = \dfrac{\text{variation between group means}}{\text{variation within groups}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{MSG}}{\mathrm{MSE}}$

Each **mean square** is a sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom.

Key idea: if $H_0$ is true, both mean squares estimate the same variance and $F$ should be near $1$.
cards.searchQuery: F statistic ANOVA between over within group variation

cards.title: A one-way ANOVA compares $4$ groups with $40$ observations in total. How many numerator (between-group) degrees of freedom?
cards.body:
$3$.

$\mathrm{df}_{\text{between}} = k - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3$.

Tip: the denominator degrees of freedom are $N - k = 40 - 4 = 36$.
cards.searchQuery: ANOVA numerator degrees of freedom k minus 1

cards.title: A one-way ANOVA compares $4$ groups with $40$ observations in total. How many denominator (within-group) degrees of freedom?
cards.body:
$36$.

$\mathrm{df}_{\text{within}} = N - k = 40 - 4 = 36$.

Watch out: the two degrees of freedom are $(k - 1,\ N - k) = (3, 36)$; swapping them gives the wrong $F$ table entry.
cards.searchQuery: ANOVA denominator degrees of freedom N minus k

cards.title: In a one-way ANOVA, what does a large $F$ statistic (and a small p-value) suggest?
cards.body:
The group means differ more than the within-group variation would explain.

The p-value is the **upper-tail** area of the $F$ distribution, because only large values of $F$ are evidence against $H_0$.

Watch out: a significant $F$ says that some means differ, not which ones.
cards.searchQuery: large F statistic small p-value ANOVA interpretation upper tail

cards.title: What conditions should hold for a one-way ANOVA $F$ test?
cards.body:
Independent random samples, roughly normal groups, and similar spreads.

- **Independent**: random samples or random assignment, with independent observations.
- **Normal**: each group is roughly normal, or the samples are large.
- **Equal variability**: the group standard deviations are similar (a common check: the largest is less than twice the smallest).

Tip: ANOVA is fairly robust to mild departures from normality when the group sizes are equal.
cards.searchQuery: ANOVA conditions independence normality equal variances

cards.title: After a significant ANOVA $F$ test, how do you find which group means differ?
cards.body:
Use a post hoc multiple-comparison procedure, such as Tukey's HSD.

These procedures compare pairs of means while controlling the **overall** error rate across all the comparisons.

Watch out: running ordinary two-sample $t$ tests on every pair brings back the inflated Type I error that ANOVA was meant to avoid.
cards.searchQuery: ANOVA post hoc test Tukey HSD which means differ

cards.title: A two-group ANOVA and a pooled two-sample $t$ test are run on the same data, with $t = 3$. What is $F$?
cards.body:
$9$.

With two groups, $F = t^2 = 3^2 = 9$, and the p-values are identical.

Key idea: ANOVA with two groups is the **pooled** two-sample $t$ test in disguise.
cards.searchQuery: ANOVA two groups F equals t squared pooled t test

cards.title: A chi-square goodness-of-fit test compares data across $6$ categories. How many degrees of freedom?
cards.body:
$5$.

$\mathrm{df} = (\text{number of categories}) - 1 = 6 - 1 = 5$.

Watch out: for a test of independence, use $(r-1)(c-1)$ instead.
cards.searchQuery: chi-square goodness of fit degrees of freedom categories minus 1

cards.title: A die is rolled $120$ times. Under the hypothesis that it is fair, what is the expected count for each face?
cards.body:
$20$.

$E = n \times p_0 = 120 \times \dfrac{1}{6} = 20$.

Tip: expected counts come from the **null hypothesis**, not from the data, so they need not be whole numbers.
cards.searchQuery: chi-square goodness of fit expected count fair die

cards.title: What is the formula for the chi-square test statistic?
cards.body:
$\chi^2 = \sum \dfrac{(O - E)^2}{E}$, summed over every category or cell.

Here $O$ is the **observed** count and $E$ the expected count under $H_0$. Each term measures how far one cell is from expectation.

Watch out: use counts, never percentages or proportions, in the formula.
cards.searchQuery: chi-square test statistic formula observed expected counts

cards.title: A cell has observed count $O = 30$ and expected count $E = 20$. What is its contribution $\dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E}$ to $\chi^2$?
cards.body:
$5$.

$\dfrac{(30 - 20)^2}{20} = \dfrac{100}{20} = 5$.

Tip: the cells with the largest contributions are where the data depart most from $H_0$.
cards.searchQuery: chi-square cell contribution observed minus expected squared over expected

cards.title: In a test of independence, a cell has row total $60$ and column total $50$, and the table total is $200$. What is the expected count for that cell?
cards.body:
$15$.

$E = \dfrac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{\text{table total}} = \dfrac{60 \times 50}{200} = 15$.

Key idea: if the variables are independent, the cell's share of the table equals the product of its row share and column share.
cards.searchQuery: chi-square independence expected count row total times column total

cards.title: What conditions should hold for a chi-square test?
cards.body:
Random data, independent observations, and all expected counts at least $5$.

Check the **expected** counts, not the observed ones. If some are too small, combine categories or use an exact test.

Watch out: the observations must be counts of individuals, each in exactly one category.
cards.searchQuery: chi-square test conditions expected counts at least 5

cards.title: What are $H_0$ and $H_a$ in a chi-square test of independence?
cards.body:
$H_0$: the two categorical variables are independent. $H_a$: they are associated.

Independence means that knowing one variable tells you nothing about the **distribution** of the other.

Watch out: a significant result shows association, not causation, and not its strength or direction.
cards.searchQuery: chi-square test of independence null alternative hypotheses association

cards.title: How does a chi-square test of homogeneity differ from a test of independence?
cards.body:
Homogeneity compares the distribution of one categorical variable across several populations; independence tests two variables within one sample.

The **calculations are identical**; what differs is the sampling design and the wording of the hypotheses.

Example: surveying three separately sampled schools about lunch preferences is homogeneity; sampling one school and recording grade level and preference is independence.
cards.searchQuery: chi-square test of homogeneity versus independence difference

cards.title: Why is the p-value of a chi-square test found from the upper tail only?
cards.body:
Because $\chi^2 \ge 0$ and any departure from $H_0$, in either direction, makes it larger.

Only large values of $\chi^2$ are evidence against $H_0$. A value near $0$ means the data match the expected counts closely.

Watch out: the **chi-square** distribution is right-skewed, so there is no left tail to double.
cards.searchQuery: chi-square test p-value upper tail right-skewed large values

cards.title: Which four features should you describe when interpreting a scatterplot?
cards.body:
Direction, form, strength and unusual features.

- **Direction**: positive or negative association.
- **Form**: linear or curved.
- **Strength**: how closely the points follow the pattern.
- **Unusual features**: outliers, clusters, gaps.

Tip: always look at the scatterplot before computing $r$, since $r$ only makes sense for linear patterns.
cards.searchQuery: scatterplot describe direction form strength unusual features

cards.title: A least-squares line with a positive slope has $R^2 = 0.49$. What is $r$?
cards.body:
$0.7$.

$r = \pm\sqrt{R^2} = \pm 0.7$, and the sign matches the slope, so $r = +0.7$.

Watch out: $R^2$ alone cannot tell you the **direction** of the association; the sign of the slope does.
cards.searchQuery: r from r squared sign of slope correlation coefficient

cards.title: The least-squares line is $\hat{y} = 20 + 3x$. What is the predicted $y$ when $x = 12$?
cards.body:
$56$.

$\hat{y} = 20 + 3(12) = 20 + 36 = 56$.

Tip: a prediction is an average for all individuals with that $x$, not a guarantee for any one individual.
cards.searchQuery: regression line prediction substitute x value predicted y

cards.title: Why is it risky to use a regression line to predict $y$ for an $x$ far outside the range of the data?
cards.body:
The linear pattern may not continue beyond the observed range.

This is **extrapolation**. A line fitted to heights of children, for example, would predict absurd heights at age $40$.

Watch out: a high $R^2$ does not make extrapolated predictions trustworthy.
cards.searchQuery: extrapolation regression risky predict outside range of data

cards.title: A regression of exam score ($y$, points) on hours studied ($x$) gives $\hat{y} = 25 + 4.5x$. How do you interpret the slope?
cards.body:
Each additional hour of study is associated with an increase of $4.5$ points in the predicted score, on average.

Always include the **units**, the words "predicted" or "on average", and the context.

Watch out: do not say that studying one more hour causes a $4.5$-point gain unless the data come from a randomized experiment.
cards.searchQuery: interpret slope regression line context units predicted change

cards.title: What does a curved pattern in a residual plot tell you about a linear model?
cards.body:
A straight line is not an appropriate model: the true relationship is curved.

A good fit shows a **random scatter** of residuals around $0$ with no pattern. A curve means the form is wrong, and a funnel shape means the spread changes with $x$.

Tip: try a transformation (such as $\log y$) or a curved model.
cards.searchQuery: residual plot curved pattern linear model not appropriate

cards.title: For a least-squares line that includes an intercept, what is the sum of all the residuals?
cards.body:
$0$.

The least-squares line balances the points above and below it, so the positive and negative **residuals** cancel exactly.

Watch out: a sum of $0$ does not mean the fit is good; it holds for every least-squares line, good or bad.
cards.searchQuery: sum of residuals least squares line equals zero

cards.title: What is an influential point in regression, and how can you spot one?
cards.body:
A point whose removal noticeably changes the slope or intercept.

Points far from $\bar{x}$ in the $x$ direction have **high leverage** and often pull the line toward them. Refit the line with and without the point to check.

Watch out: an outlier in $y$ near the middle of the $x$ values changes the intercept but barely changes the slope.
cards.searchQuery: influential point high leverage regression outlier effect on slope

cards.title: A regression slope has $b_1 = 2.4$ with standard error $0.8$. What is the $t$ statistic for $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$?
cards.body:
$3$.

$t = \dfrac{b_1 - 0}{\mathrm{SE}_{b_1}} = \dfrac{2.4}{0.8} = 3$.

Tip: $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ says that there is no **linear** relationship between $x$ and $y$ in the population.
cards.searchQuery: t statistic regression slope test beta 1 zero

cards.title: A regression of $y$ on $x$ uses $n = 27$ data points. How many degrees of freedom does the $t$ test for the slope have?
cards.body:
$25$.

$\mathrm{df} = n - 2 = 27 - 2 = 25$.

Why: two parameters, the slope and the intercept, are estimated from the data, so two degrees of freedom are lost.
cards.searchQuery: regression slope t test degrees of freedom n minus 2

cards.title: What does the LINE acronym stand for in the conditions for regression inference?
cards.body:
Linear, Independent, Normal, Equal variance.

- **Linear**: the true relationship is linear (check the residual plot).
- **Independent**: the observations are independent.
- **Normal**: the residuals are roughly normal for each $x$.
- **Equal variance**: the spread of the residuals is the same at every $x$.

Mnemonic: LINE, the four conditions for a line to be a good model for inference.
cards.searchQuery: LINE conditions regression inference linear independent normal equal variance

cards.title: A regression has $\mathrm{SSE} = 100$ (the sum of squared residuals) and $n = 27$. What is the residual standard deviation $s_e = \sqrt{\mathrm{SSE}/(n-2)}$?
cards.body:
$2$.

$s_e = \sqrt{\dfrac{100}{27 - 2}} = \sqrt{4} = 2$.

Tip: $s_e$ estimates the typical size of a prediction error, in the units of $y$.
cards.searchQuery: residual standard deviation regression SSE n minus 2

cards.title: A regression has total variation $\mathrm{SST} = 200$ and unexplained variation $\mathrm{SSE} = 50$. What is $R^2$?
cards.body:
$0.75$.

$R^2 = 1 - \dfrac{\mathrm{SSE}}{\mathrm{SST}} = 1 - \dfrac{50}{200} = 0.75$.

Key idea: $R^2$ is the fraction of the total variation in $y$ that the model explains, since $\mathrm{SST} = \mathrm{SSR} + \mathrm{SSE}$.
cards.searchQuery: R squared from SSE and SST regression explained variation

cards.title: A regression has $b_1 = 1.5$ and $\mathrm{SE}_{b_1} = 0.5$. Using $t^* = 2.0$, what is the lower endpoint of the confidence interval for the true slope?
cards.body:
$0.5$.

$b_1 \pm t^*\,\mathrm{SE}_{b_1} = 1.5 \pm 2.0(0.5) = 1.5 \pm 1.0 = (0.5,\ 2.5)$.

Tip: because the interval excludes $0$, the test of $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ would reject at the matching level.
cards.searchQuery: confidence interval for regression slope worked example t critical value

cards.title: In a multiple regression of $y$ on $x_1$ and $x_2$, how do you interpret the coefficient of $x_1$?
cards.body:
It is the predicted change in $y$ for a $1$-unit increase in $x_1$, **holding $x_2$ constant**.

Because the other variable is held fixed, the coefficient of $x_1$ can differ from the slope in a simple regression of $y$ on $x_1$ alone.

Watch out: adding variables never lowers $R^2$; use adjusted $R^2$ to compare models of different sizes.
cards.searchQuery: multiple regression coefficient interpretation holding other variables constant
